The Long-tailed duck (Clangula hyemalis) begins life as a relatively heavy egg, with freshly laid clutches yielding an initial wet weight of 43 grams [Ww0 = 43 grams] for the newly deposited zygote. Incubation, a demanding physiological process for the attending female, proceeds at an average nest temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C]; under these thermal conditions, development from ovum to hatching requires an incubation period of 25 days [ab = 25 days]. At the moment of hatching, the precocial chicks emerge with a wet weight at birth of 27.75 grams [Wwb = 27.75 grams], a mass that represents a substantial fraction of the egg's original contents. This relatively advanced state at hatching is characteristic of sea ducks and allows the downy young to leave the nest scrape within hours of emergence, though they remain dependent on maternal brooding for thermoregulation during the first several days of life. The energetic demands of both incubation and chick rearing place considerable pressure on the breeding female, whose body condition is a critical determinant of reproductive success in this arctic-nesting species.

During the post-hatching period, the strictly controlled thermal environment of the nest gives way to the variable conditions of the tundra. At the active metabolic temperature typical of the species, which is 41 °C [T = 41 °C], the young reach the critical stage of fledging at 35 days after hatching [tx = 35 days after hatching]. This relatively rapid development to flight capability is an adaptation to the short Arctic summer, enabling the juveniles to depart breeding grounds before the onset of winter. The subsequent transition to the juvenile stage involves a period of intense foraging to build the body mass necessary for both migration and the onset of sexual maturation. The attainment of puberty, defined by the development of functional gonads and reached at approximately 100 days after hatching [tp = approximately 100 days after hatching], allows individuals to attain physiological adulthood within a single growing season, a hallmark of the life history strategy of this high-lat at a temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]itude sea duck.

Sexual size dimorphism is pronounced in Clangula hyemalis, with adult males substantially outweighing their female counterparts. The ultimate wet weight for adult males reaches 661 grams [Wwi = 661 grams], a value that reflects the energetic investment in both the species' elaborate breeding plumage and the maintenance of a large body size necessary for thermoregulation in frigid waters. Females, by contrast, attain a smaller adult body mass, with an ultimate wet weight of 636 grams [Wwi = 636 grams]. This disparity in mass is typical of many sea duck species and is thought to be driven by the contrasting selective pressures acting on each sex; males benefit from larger size in intrasexual competition, while females may face constraints on body mass imposed by the energetic costs of egg production and the demands of prolonged incubation. These adult masses are reached only after the completion of somatic growth, which in this species occurs well after the onset of reproductive maturity.

Reproductive effort in the Long-tailed duck is constrained by the brevity of the Arctic breeding season. Field studies indicate that females produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], with each clutch containing between 4 to 11 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 4 to 11 eggs per clutch]. This clutch size range, measured under the active metabolic temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C], represents a substantial reproductive investment given the relatively small body size of the female. The timing of first reproduction is deferred relative to the attainment of puberty, a life-history pattern often interpreted as allowing additional time for the development of foraging skills and the establishment of a stable territory. The time since birth at first brood, or the age at which a female successfully hatches her first clutch, is 730 days since birth [tR = 730 days since birth], meaning that most individuals do not breed until their second calendar year of life at a temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. This delayed breeding is common among sea ducks and is associated with low annual adult mortality.

Longevity data for the Long-tailed duck come primarily from long-term banding studies conducted on the wintering grounds. The species exhibits a remarkably extended lifespan for a bird of its body size, with the oldest documented individuals living for approximately 22.7 years [am = approximately 22.7 years] when measured at the species' active metabolic temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. This impressive maximum longevity, exceeding two decades, is coupled with the low annual reproductive output described above, resulting in a characteristically slow life history pace. Comparative analyses within the tribe Mergini suggest that this combination of high adult survival and low fecundity is an evolutionary response to the unpredictable and resource-limited environment of the Arctic breeding grounds. The capacity for such sustained survival is supported by the bird's efficient foraging ecology and its ability to exploit a wide range of marine invertebrate prey across its circumpolar distribution. These life history traits make the species particularly vulnerable to environmental perturbations that affect adult survival rates.
